title: AGPAL Accreditation
description: Learn how AGPAL accreditation relates to patient safety, quality, privacy and continuous improvement at our practice.
headings: What accreditation does — and does not — tell you.
Why this matters at Woolloongabba Medical Centre.
text: Accredited General Practice Why AGPAL accreditation matters. A plain-language explanation of what independent general practice accreditation means for patients, and how it supports safer, more reliable care. Accreditation in plain language. General practice accreditation is an independent assessment of the systems a practice uses to support safe and quality care. In Australia, accreditation under the National General Practice Accreditation Scheme assesses practices against the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) Standards for general practices. It is not an advertising award and it is not a guarantee that every consultation will have a particular outcome. It means the practice has demonstrated that important systems, responsibilities and safeguards are in place and have been independently assessed against national requirements. Our current status. Woolloongabba Medical Centre is listed on the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care register as an accredited general practice at 468 Vulture Street, Woolloongabba, with accreditation recorded through 22 March 2029 . Accreditation status checked against the national register on 7 October 2026. The standard used today. As at October 2026, the National General Practice Accreditation Scheme continues to assess practices against the RACGP Standards for general practices, 5th edition. The 6th edition has been released and practices are being encouraged to use its guidance as they review and improve their systems. Patient safety. Accreditation looks beyond the consultation room. It considers whether a practice has dependable systems to reduce avoidable harm and respond when something does not go as planned. For patients, this can include safe and well-maintained equipment, appropriately trained staff, reliable patient identification, safe medicine and vaccine handling, emergency arrangements, clear follow-up processes and systems for managing clinical risk. The purpose is practical: important safety steps should be built into everyday practice rather than depend on memory or individual habit. Healthcare quality. Quality in general practice is not only about clinical knowledge. It also depends on how care is organised, communicated and followed through over time. The RACGP Standards cover areas such as patient-centred communication, informed decisions, respectful care, accessibility, comprehensive care, clinical handover, health records, practitioner qualifications and the safe use of medicines. Accreditation assesses whether the practice has systems that support these expectations consistently. This helps create a more reliable experience for patients across appointments, practitioners and different stages of care. Clinical governance. Clinical governance is the framework that makes clear who is responsible for safety and quality, how risks are managed and how the practice learns from problems. In patient terms, it means there should be clear responsibilities, appropriate staff training, documented policies, effective teamwork, incident and risk management, emergency planning and oversight of systems that affect care. Good governance does not remove clinical judgement. It provides the structure around clinical care so that responsibilities are understood and important safety issues are identified, escalated and addressed. Infection prevention. General practices need systems that reduce the risk of infection for patients, staff and visitors. Accreditation includes requirements relating to infection prevention and control, including sterilisation and the safe handling of clinical equipment where applicable. In practice, this can involve hand hygiene, cleaning, reprocessing or sterilising reusable equipment, safe sharps and waste handling, maintaining a suitable clinical environment, and protecting vaccine potency through appropriate storage and temperature control. These processes are part of routine patient safety, even when they are not visible during an appointment. Patient privacy. Health information is highly sensitive. Accreditation standards require practices to have systems for confidentiality, privacy, secure health records and information security. For patients, this means the practice should control who can access clinical information, protect records from inappropriate access or disclosure, manage conversations and communications with appropriate privacy, and explain how personal health information is handled. Accreditation works alongside Australian privacy law and professional confidentiality obligations; it does not replace them. Continuous improvement. Accreditation is not intended to be a one-time inspection followed by business as usual. The standards require practices to undertake quality-improvement activities and use information, feedback and experience to strengthen care. This may include reviewing patient feedback and complaints, examining incidents or near misses, auditing clinical data, improving administrative processes, updating policies, strengthening follow-up systems and measuring whether changes have actually helped. The important principle is that a practice should be able to identify opportunities to improve, act on them and learn from the result. What accreditation does — and does not — tell you. It does tell you The practice has been independently assessed against nationally recognised general practice safety and quality standards. It does not guarantee A particular diagnosis, treatment result, waiting time or individual experience at every visit. It does tell you Important systems for governance, privacy, infection prevention, risk management and quality improvement are part of the assessment. text: Patient Information Healthcare FAQ Hub Clear, patient-first answers to common questions about visiting the practice, arranging care and understanding what happens next. FAQ categories Find the answer you need. Choose a topic below. Each answer links to the detailed patient or service page if you need more information. Search FAQs All Appointments New Patients Fees & Medicare Results & Scripts Telehealth Referrals After Hours Services Practice Information Appointments New Patients Fees & Medicare Results & Scripts Telehealth Referrals After Hours Care Healthcare Services Practice Information Appointments How do I book an appointment? Appointments can be booked online through HotDoc or by calling reception on (07) 3217 3344. Book an appointment → When should I consider a longer appointment? A longer appointment may be helpful if you have several concerns, a complex health history, a mental health discussion or forms that require clinical review. If you are unsure, ask reception about the available appointment types. Booking information → What if I need to change or cancel an appointment? Contact reception as early as possible if your plans change so the appointment can be released for another patient. Appointment options → What if I am not sure which appointment type to choose? Reception can explain the available appointment types and appointment lengths. Clinical decisions about your care are made by your practitioner. Appointment options → Back to top ↑ New Patients Are new patients welcome? Yes. Woolloongabba Medical Centre welcomes new patients and families. The New Patients page explains how to prepare for a first visit. New patient information → What should I bring to my first appointment? Bring your Medicare card or Medicare details, any relevant concession card, an up-to-date medication list and relevant medical information such as recent letters, reports or results if available. What to bring → Can members of the same family attend the practice? Yes. Many families choose the same practice for convenience and continuity, while each person’s healthcare information and privacy remain individual. Family Health → How can I prepare if I have a longer or more complex medical history? Bring a current medication list and any recent specialist letters, reports or results that may help your practitioner understand your care. Your practitioner can advise if any additional information is needed. Preparing for your first visit → Back to top ↑ Fees & Medicare Do you bulk bill? Woolloongabba Medical Centre provides 100% Medicare bulk billing for standard Medicare-eligible general practice consultations for patients with a valid Medicare card. Bulk billing information → Can some services still have a fee? Yes. Fees may apply to procedures, medical reports, employment or occupational medicals and other non-Medicare services. Where a fee applies, patients are advised in advance wherever practical. Fees & billing → What should I bring for Medicare? Bring your current Medicare card or Medicare details and any relevant concession information. Medicare information → How can I check whether a fee applies before my appointment? Review the Fees & Billing information or contact reception before your appointment. Where a fee applies, the practice aims to explain it in advance wherever practical. Fees & billing → Back to top ↑ Results & Scripts How are test results managed? Follow the instructions given by your doctor or our team. Some results require a consultation so they can be interpreted in the context of your health and the next steps can be discussed. Test results information → What should I do if I am worried about a result? If you are concerned about a result or your symptoms are changing, contact the practice for advice rather than waiting for a routine follow-up. For a life-threatening emergency, call Triple Zero (000). Test results information → Can I request a repeat prescription without an appointment? Prescription requirements depend on the medication and your clinical circumstances. A doctor may require a consultation or review before prescribing. Repeat prescription information → Why might my doctor ask to review me before issuing a prescription? Safe prescribing may require an up-to-date review of your condition, medicines, monitoring or other clinical information. The required follow-up depends on your individual circumstances and the medicine involved. Repeat prescription information → Back to top ↑ Telehealth Do you provide telehealth appointments? Telehealth may be available for selected healthcare needs where a remote consultation is clinically suitable. Telehealth information → Can every health concern be managed by telehealth? No. Some concerns require a physical examination, observations, testing, a procedure or another form of in-person assessment. Telehealth service → Is telehealth covered by Medicare? Medicare eligibility depends on current rules, the appointment type and your individual circumstances. Reception can confirm the booking and billing arrangement before the consultation. Telehealth information → What happens if my practitioner decides I need an examination? If the concern cannot be safely assessed remotely, you may be asked to attend the medical centre or another appropriate in-person service. Telehealth information → Back to top ↑ Referrals How do referrals work? A GP can assess whether a referral is appropriate and prepare one when clinically indicated. The referral should contain the information needed by the receiving specialist or service. Referral information → Do I need an appointment to discuss a referral? A consultation may be required so the doctor can understand the reason for referral, review relevant information and make an appropriate clinical decision. Referral information → Can reception issue or renew a referral for me? No. A referral is a clinical document and must be considered by a doctor. Reception can help you arrange the appropriate appointment. Referral information → Back to top ↑ After Hours Care What should I do if I need medical care after the practice is closed? When the practice is closed, patients who need after-hours medical assistance can contact Hello Home Doctor on 134 100. The After Hours Care page explains other available pathways. After Hours Care → What should I do in a medical emergency? For a life-threatening illness or injury, call Triple Zero (000) or attend the nearest emergency department. Do not wait for a routine appointment. Emergency and after-hours information → Can I call 13 HEALTH for advice? Yes. Queenslanders can call 13 HEALTH on 13 43 25 84 for health assessment and advice from registered nurses, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. After Hours Care → Back to top ↑ Healthcare Services What healthcare services are available at the practice? The practice provides general practice care across family health, women’s health, men’s health, children’s health, mental health, chronic disease care, preventive healthcare and telehealth, along with other services described on the Services page. Our Services → Do you provide chronic disease care? Yes. The practice supports people living with long-term health conditions through ongoing general practice care, monitoring and coordinated planning. Chronic Disease Care → Can I discuss preventive healthcare with my GP? Yes. Preventive healthcare can include health assessments, screening discussions, vaccination, cardiovascular risk review and lifestyle support based on your individual circumstances. Preventive Healthcare → How can I find a practitioner with an interest relevant to my care? The Meet Our Team pages list verified practitioner qualifications, languages, areas of care and professional interests where publicly available. Reception can also help with practitioner availability. Meet Our Team → What if I am not sure which service I need? You do not need to diagnose the problem yourself before booking. Reception can explain available appointment types, and your practitioner can assess your needs and discuss appropriate next steps. Our Services → Back to top ↑ Practice Information Is parking available? Patient parking is available nearby, including disability parking for patients who require it. Access & Parking → Is Woolloongabba Medical Centre wheelchair accessible? Yes. The medical centre is designed for wheelchair access. Contact reception before attending if you have specific access or mobility needs. Accessibility information → How is my medical information protected? Patient health information is treated as confidential and kept secure. Access is limited to authorised people who need the information for legitimate healthcare or practice purposes. Confidentiality & Privacy → Does the practice use reminders or recalls? Yes. The practice uses reminder and recall processes to support preventive healthcare and clinically important follow-up. Reminder & Recall Service → How can I provide feedback or make a complaint? You can raise feedback with the practice and ask to speak with the Practice Manager. If you prefer an external pathway, the Queensland Office of the Health Ombudsman accepts health-service complaints. Feedback & Complaints → Where can I read about practice policies, patient rights, quality and safety? The Practice Information Authority Centre brings together patient rights, privacy, access, policies, infection prevention, accreditation, quality and safety information in one place. Practice Information → Back to top ↑ Still need help? Choose the next step that suits you. If your question is not answered here, use the detailed information pages or contact reception for administrative help. text: Feedback & Complaints Questions and concerns deserve a clear pathway. How to give feedback, raise a complaint and access an independent pathway if you need one. Your experience matters. We welcome compliments, suggestions, concerns and complaints. Speaking up helps us understand what is working well and where communication, systems or care pathways may need attention. Patient communications Review requests and formal feedback are different. We may use HotDoc to send a review request after care. A review request is optional and is separate from our formal feedback and complaints pathway. If you want the practice to investigate a concern, please contact us directly using the feedback and complaints pathway on this page. How to raise feedback or a complaint. Speak with reception or ask to contact the Practice Manager. Tell us what happened, what you are concerned about and what outcome you are seeking. Provide any information that may help us understand the issue. We will review the matter through the appropriate internal process and respond as soon as practical. Contact Woolloongabba Medical Centre → What happens after you raise a concern. Your concern should be considered by the appropriate person in the practice. Depending on the issue, this may involve reviewing records, speaking with relevant team members and considering whether a process, communication step or other part of care needs to change. If you prefer an independent pathway. In Queensland, the Office of the Health Ombudsman is the single entry point for complaints about health services, health practitioners and health facilities. You can contact the OHO directly if you would prefer an external complaints pathway. Office of the Health Ombudsman Phone: 133 OHO (133 646) Phone lines: Monday to Friday, 9:30am–4:00pm Make a complaint online → Feedback should not affect your care. You have the right to give feedback or make a complaint without it affecting the way you are treated. We expect concerns to be heard respectfully and handled through an appropriate process. text: Infection Prevention & Control Safety is built into everyday systems. How cleaning, clinical processes and accredited practice systems support a safer healthcare environment. Clean, safe systems support every consultation. Infection prevention is part of everyday general practice. We use routine cleaning, disinfection and clinical processes to help reduce avoidable infection risks for patients, visitors and staff. What infection prevention includes. Cleaning and disinfection of clinical and shared environments. Safe handling and reprocessing of reusable clinical equipment where applicable. Hand hygiene and standard precautions. Safe vaccine storage and cold-chain processes where vaccines are provided. Processes for sharps, clinical waste and other infection-control risks. If you may be infectious. If you have symptoms of a potentially infectious illness and are unsure how to attend safely, contact reception before arriving. We can advise on the most appropriate current pathway for your appointment. Why these systems matter. Infection prevention protects more than the person being treated. It helps protect other patients, visitors and staff, including people who may be more vulnerable to infection. Part of a broader quality system. Infection prevention sits within our wider quality and safety responsibilities. General practice accreditation includes independent assessment of practice systems against national standards and supports ongoing review and improvement. title: Patient Code of Conduct
h1: A safe and respectful environment for everyone.
description: How we maintain a safe and respectful practice for patients, visitors and staff at Woolloongabba Medical Centre. Read our shared expectations.
headings: What we ask of patients and visitors.
Behaviour that places others at risk.
text: Patient Code of Conduct A safe and respectful environment for everyone. At Woolloongabba Medical Centre, we are committed to a safe, welcoming and respectful environment for patients, visitors, healthcare professionals and staff. We ask everyone to help us uphold that commitment. Our shared commitment. Healthcare works best when people feel safe, heard and respected. This Code of Conduct describes the everyday behaviour that helps make Woolloongabba Medical Centre a considerate place to receive care and to work. It applies to patients, accompanying visitors and anyone using our shared spaces. We recognise that illness, pain, worry or difficult circumstances can affect how people feel and communicate. Our team will aim to respond calmly, listen to concerns and discuss reasonable support or accessibility arrangements where possible. What we ask of patients and visitors. Speak to practitioners, staff, other patients and visitors with courtesy and respect. Follow reasonable infection prevention and safety instructions, including advice about respiratory symptoms and hand hygiene. Share accurate health and contact information where you can, and tell your clinician when something is unclear or you need assistance. Respect other people's privacy, personal space and appointments, including in reception and waiting areas. Let reception know if you need to cancel, arrive late, require communication support or need an access adjustment. We welcome questions and understand that patients may disagree with a recommendation. You can raise a concern respectfully and ask for information about your options. Behaviour that places others at risk. To protect patients, families and our team, we do not accept: Abusive, aggressive, intimidating or threatening behaviour, including verbal or physical aggression. Harassment, bullying or discriminatory remarks or conduct. Violence, deliberate property damage or behaviour that creates an unsafe environment. Attending while significantly affected by alcohol or illicit drugs when this compromises safety or appropriate care. Refusing reasonable safety directions in a way that places others at risk. If someone's health or safety is at immediate risk, staff will prioritise an appropriate safety response. Anyone needing urgent medical attention should tell staff or seek emergency assistance; safety concerns will not be used as a substitute for appropriate clinical assessment. Children and accompanying visitors. Children are welcome at the practice. Parents and carers are asked to supervise children in waiting and shared areas, keeping entrances, corridors and clinical spaces safe and accessible. We ask accompanying visitors to respect other patients' privacy and follow staff directions about consultation rooms and shared spaces. If you need to bring a support person or have specific care or accessibility needs, please let reception know so we can discuss suitable arrangements. Mobile phones, photography and devices. Please keep phone conversations and device sounds at a considerate volume. To protect privacy, do not photograph, film or record other patients, visitors or staff without appropriate permission. Ask your clinician before making a recording during a consultation, and respect any privacy or safety arrangements that apply. Our responsibility to you. We are committed to treating people with dignity, communicating respectfully, supporting reasonable accessibility needs and protecting patient privacy. Staff and clinicians will explain relevant practice procedures and how to raise questions or feedback. We strive to respond to concerns fairly and without unnecessary confrontation. Read more about your rights and responsibilities and accessibility at the practice . If a problem occurs. When behaviour disrupts care or creates a safety concern, our team may first explain the concern, ask for the behaviour to stop, or offer a practical way to continue the conversation safely. Depending on the circumstances, we may: Ask a person to move to another area or leave the premises when it is safe and appropriate to do so. Arrange another way to communicate, schedule care or review future attendance arrangements. Contact security or police where threats, violence or serious risks make this necessary. Consider alternative ongoing care arrangements when a safe therapeutic relationship cannot be maintained, with appropriate communication and continuity-of-care planning. Decisions are made according to the situation, including clinical urgency, patient needs and relevant obligations. We will not treat the above as automatic penalties. In a medical emergency, call Triple Zero (000). Questions, feedback and concerns. If you are worried about an interaction or would like to explain a concern, please speak with reception or use our Feedback & Complaints pathway. You can also contact the practice for help with accessibility, communication or visiting arrangements. Related information. text: Patient Rights & Responsibilities Respect, information and partnership matter. A patient-friendly guide to what you can expect from care and how shared responsibilities support a safe practice environment. What you can expect from healthcare. The Australian Charter of Healthcare Rights describes seven rights that apply across Australian healthcare: access, safety, respect, partnership, information, privacy and the right to give feedback. Access Healthcare that meets your needs, within the services available. Safety Care delivered with attention to quality and a safe environment. Respect Dignity, courtesy and respect for your identity, culture, beliefs and choices. Partnership The opportunity to ask questions and be involved in decisions about your care. Information Clear information about your healthcare, options, costs and next steps. Privacy Respect for personal privacy and confidential health information. Give feedback The ability to provide feedback or make a complaint without it affecting how you are treated. Read the Australian Charter of Healthcare Rights → Shared responsibilities support safer care. Treat staff, clinicians and other patients with courtesy and respect. Provide accurate information about your health, medications and relevant history. Ask questions if you do not understand information or instructions. Attend appointments on time where possible, or let us know if you need to cancel. Follow agreed next steps, including tests, referrals, results review and follow-up appointments. Tell us if your contact information changes. Respect is expected in both directions. We do not accept abusive, threatening or violent behaviour toward patients, practitioners or staff. A respectful environment helps everyone feel safe and supports effective healthcare. Related information. description: Why Woolloongabba Medical Centre values continuity, trust, family healthcare and long-term relationships.
text: Our Philosophy of Care A long view of healthcare. We believe the strongest care grows from relationships — knowing the person, understanding the context and remaining present through more than one moment in their health. Healthcare built on relationships We believe healthcare is more than treating illness. Healthcare works best when practitioners understand the person behind the appointment and can bring context from previous care into the next conversation. Strong healthcare relationships support continuity, greater understanding and more personalised care over time. What guides our care Trust Continuity Connection Community Long-term wellbeing Our approach also values holistic care, health promotion, disease prevention, dignity and respect for every patient. Healthcare with continuity Patients often choose a healthcare practice because of convenience. Many stay because of relationships. At Woolloongabba Medical Centre, we believe continuity of care creates a more connected patient experience because a person’s history, goals and circumstances can be understood over time. text: Confidentiality & Privacy Your information deserves careful protection. A plain-English guide to how personal health information is handled and how you can ask questions about your records. Your health information is private. Your medical record contains personal and health information that is important to your care. We treat that information as confidential and limit access to authorised people who need it for legitimate healthcare or practice purposes. What may be held in your record. Your record can include identification and contact details, Medicare information, medical history, medications, allergies, consultation notes, results, referrals and other information needed to provide or coordinate your healthcare. How information is used and shared. Health information is used to provide and coordinate your care and to support the safe operation of the practice. Information may also need to be shared when you consent, when another healthcare provider needs information for your care, or when disclosure is otherwise authorised or required. We aim to share only what is reasonably needed for the purpose. Accessing or correcting your information. You can ask about information held in your record and request access to your health information. If you believe information is inaccurate, you can ask us to correct it or record your concern. Some limits can apply where disclosure would affect another person’s privacy or create a serious risk. Keeping information secure. Privacy depends on everyday systems as well as professional confidentiality. Access controls, staff responsibilities, secure clinical systems and appropriate handling of documents and messages all contribute to protecting patient information. Patient communications HotDoc is one of our patient communication partners. We use HotDoc to support patient communications such as appointment reminders, recall and result messages, digital forms, review requests and payment requests. HotDoc provides the communication platform; questions about your healthcare, results, billing or records should still be directed to Woolloongabba Medical Centre. We also use a separate, consent-based AI-assisted transcription process in some consultations. You can read how consent and clinician oversight work on our AI-Assisted Consultation Notes page . Digital Reception and website questions. Digital Reception is designed to help visitors find information already published on this website. The production version uses a local website-content index and does not access your medical record or search the public internet. Please do not enter personal, clinical or sensitive health information into Digital Reception. Privacy questions or concerns. If you have a privacy question, want to request access to information, believe something is inaccurate or want to raise a concern about how information has been handled, contact the practice and ask to speak with the Practice Manager. Clinical governance Clear responsibilities, policies and processes supporting safe healthcare. Privacy Confidential and appropriate handling of personal health information. text: Reminder & Recall Service Continuity includes knowing what comes next. How reminders and recalls support preventive healthcare, clinically important follow-up and continuity of care. Preventive healthcare is easier when follow-up is planned. We use reminders and recalls to support preventive healthcare and clinically important follow-up. Depending on your circumstances, we may contact you when a vaccination, screening activity, review or other follow-up may be due. Patient communications Reminders and recalls may be sent through HotDoc. We use HotDoc as a patient communication partner for appointment reminders, preventive-health recalls and other follow-up messages. These communications help us prompt patients when care may be due, but they do not replace the follow-up plan your doctor has given you. Keep your mobile number and email address current so important practice communications can reach you. What is the difference between a reminder and a recall? A reminder may let you know that routine preventive care, such as a vaccination or screening activity, may be due. A recall may be used when your treating clinician or the practice needs you to return for clinically important follow-up. The exact reason will depend on your care. What the service may cover. Vaccinations and immunisations. Screening and preventive health activities. Follow-up requested by your treating clinician. Ongoing monitoring where follow-up forms part of your care plan. Keep your contact details current. Reminder and recall systems work best when we have your current contact information. Please tell reception if your phone number, address or other important contact details change. Do not wait for a reminder if you have already been given a plan. If your doctor asks you to return, arrange a test, review a result or seek care if symptoms change, follow those instructions even if you have not received a reminder or recall. title: Why Team-Based Care Matters
description: How continuity, communication, coordinated healthcare and practical support work together at Woolloongabba Medical Centre.
headings: Healthcare is more than one consultation.
Continuity of care gives healthcare context.
Patient support includes the practical parts of healthcare.
Coordinated healthcare matters most when care becomes complex.
text: Team-Based Care Why team-based care matters. Healthcare is stronger when the people and systems around a patient work together. Healthcare is more than one consultation. Good healthcare often involves more than one person and more than one appointment. A general practitioner may lead clinical decision-making, while nursing, allied health, reception and practice management support different parts of the patient journey. The value comes from those roles working as one practice rather than as separate services. Continuity of care gives healthcare context. When care is followed over time, new symptoms, medicines, test results, referrals and life changes can be understood in the context of what is already known. Where possible, seeing a familiar GP can reduce repetition and help longer-term plans remain connected. Familiar history Previous consultations and health information can give new concerns more context. Clearer follow-up Results, referrals and care plans are easier to connect when the practice can follow what happens next. Long-term perspective Prevention and chronic care often benefit from decisions made across months and years rather than one visit at a time. Support when circumstances change Shared practice systems help the wider team support the next step if your usual practitioner is unavailable. Communication helps care stay coordinated. Different healthcare professionals may contribute at different stages. Team-based care helps make responsibilities clearer: who is assessing a concern, who is supporting treatment, what follow-up is needed and when another service or specialist should become involved. Appropriate information sharing within the practice is guided by privacy, confidentiality and each team member’s role in your care. Patient support includes the practical parts of healthcare. Reliable care also depends on what happens around the consultation. Reception helps patients reach the right appointment pathway. Nursing may support treatment-room and preventive care. Practice management maintains systems for privacy, quality, feedback and day-to-day operations. Allied health can add focused support where appropriate. These roles do not replace the relationship between patient and clinician. They help that relationship work more reliably. Coordinated healthcare matters most when care becomes complex. People living with several health conditions, taking multiple medicines, recovering from illness or injury, or moving between general practice, allied health and specialist services may need several parts of the healthcare system at once. A well-organised practice helps patients understand the next step and keeps care connected wherever possible. Meet the healthcare organisation. title: AI Transcription & Consent
description: Understand AI-assisted consultation transcription, patient consent and what to expect at Woolloongabba Medical Centre.
headings: What may happen during the consultation
text: Practice Information AI-Assisted Consultation Notes & Consent Some doctors may use AI-assisted transcription to help prepare consultation notes. It is used only with your consent and never replaces your doctor’s clinical judgement. What this technology does AI-assisted transcription, sometimes called an AI scribe, can listen to a consultation and help prepare a draft transcript or clinical note. It is a documentation aid. It does not diagnose you, decide your treatment or replace the conversation between you and your doctor. Your consent comes first Before an AI-assisted transcription service is used, your doctor will explain that it is being proposed and ask for your consent. You can say no. Declining does not affect your ability to receive care at Woolloongabba Medical Centre. What may happen during the consultation Depending on the service being used, consultation audio may be processed to create a draft transcript or note. Your doctor remains responsible for checking the information, correcting it where needed and finalising the clinical record. Privacy and health information Health information is sensitive. We expect AI-assisted documentation tools used in the practice to be considered within our privacy, security and clinical-governance processes. You may ask your doctor which service is being used and what information it processes. We do not make provider-specific storage or retention claims on this page unless they have been verified for the service in use. You can change your mind If you consent and then become uncomfortable, tell your doctor. They can stop using the transcription service where practicable and continue the consultation without it. Human review remains essential AI-generated transcripts and draft notes can be incomplete or inaccurate. Your doctor reviews the output and remains responsible for the clinical record and the care decisions made during your consultation. Questions patients often ask Do I have to agree to AI-assisted transcription? No. You can decline. Your consultation and access to care can continue without the transcription service. Does the AI make clinical decisions? No. The technology assists with documentation. Your doctor remains responsible for clinical judgement, decisions and the final medical record. Can I ask which AI service is being used? Yes. You can ask your doctor what service is being used and how it is intended to support documentation during your consultation. What if I change my mind after I consent? Tell your doctor. They can stop using the transcription service where practicable and continue the consultation without it. Where can I read more about privacy? Read our Confidentiality & Privacy information or speak with the Practice Manager if you have a question about how your information is handled.
